1.Introduction
The study of efficiency in pure-exchange economies has served as the foundation for the char-
acterization of Pareto-optimal (PO) allocations of an aggregate endowment among a population
of economic agents. The historical roots of this field can be traced back to the seminal work of
Borch (1960, 1962) and Wilson (1968), within the framework of Expected Utility (EU) Theory
with risk-averse agents. Under this framework, the celebrated Borch rule states that an allocation
is PO if and only if the ratio of marginal utilities between the agents is constant. Furthermore, op-
timal allocations are non-decreasing deterministic functions of the aggregate endowment. In other

In the above literature on optimal consumption, or optimal allocations, in a dynamic framework,
Paretoefficiencyisdefinedfromtheperspectiveoftime-0preferences. Futureconsumptionstreams,
future endowment streams, or future risk profiles are first discounted to time0, and then evaluated.
Our contention is that this leads to an inherently myopic view that fails to capture the dynamic
structure of endowment profiles. We propose a novel approach that allows to incorporate the
dynamic structure of risk profiles into the decision-making process, through dynamic risk measures;
and we introduce the associated notions of dynamic individual rationality and dynamic Pareto
optimality.
Specifically, in this paper, we assume that each agent’s initial endowment is given by a discrete-
time stochastic process, and the initial endowments are aggregated and reallocated at each point
in time. Moreover, agent preferences over discrete-time stochastic processes are represented by
strongly time-consistent dynamic risk measures, which are extensively studied in the risk manage-
ment literature (Cheridito et al., 2006; Ruszczyński, 2010; Bielecki et al., 2018; Moresco et al., 2024;
Coache and Jaimungal, 2024; Dentcheva and Ruszczynski, 2024; Pesenti et al., 2025; Bielecki et al.,
2025). Unlike the existing literature on recursive utilities, we assume that agent preferences are
(conditionally) translation invariant, which is a classical assumption for risk measures. Therefore,
the risk of a deterministic endowment is equal to the size of the endowment and agent preferences
admit a recursive representation, as in Cheridito et al. (2006) and Ruszczyński (2010). This recur-
sive representation allows us to define a notion of optimality for all time points, contrasting with
classical notions of efficiency which are defined from the perspective of time0only, and hence are
inherently myopic. Our new notion of optimality, which we calldynamic Pareto optimality(or just
Pareto optimality for simplicity), not only considers the risk of an allocation process at time0, but
also incorporates the dynamic structure of risk profiles into the decision-making process.
In our first main result (Theorem 4.3), we show that an allocation is PO if and only if it is the
solution to a series of recursive (backward in time) optimization problems. When the problem is
static, we recover the classical result that PO allocations optimize a given social welfare function.
In Section 5, we extend the classical notion of comonotonicity to the dynamic setting and derive a
comonotone improvement theorem for dynamic risk measures that preserve the convex order. We
further study Pareto optima in the comonotone market, and we show that each PO allocation in
the comonotone market is also PO in the unconstrained market, therefore providing justification
for studying the comonotone market. Our second main result (Theorem 5.21) provides a crisp
characterization of comonotone Pareto optima when agent preferences are coherent and satisfy a
property that we callequidistribution-preserving. This allows for a useful algorithmic implemen-
tation, which we demonstrate for a two-period setting in Section 6.2. Our numerical example
highlights the differences between dynamic and static models, and it demonstrates how future risks
affect allocations in earlier periods.
The rest of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 introduces the necessary notation
and recalls some relevant properties of dynamic risk measures. Section 3 presents the dynamic
optimal-allocation problem and defines a notion of Pareto optimality for this framework. Section
4 characterizes Pareto optima, and our main characterization of comonotone Pareto optima is
provided in Section 5. A numerical example is provided in Section 6, and Section 7 concludes.
Some background material is presented in Appendix A.

In this paper, we study Pareto optima in a discrete-time multi-period pure-exchange economy,
whereagentshavepreferencesoverstochasticendowmentprocessesthatarerepresentedbystrongly
time-consistentdynamicriskmeasures, whichhavebeenextensivelystudiedintheriskmanagement

the perspective of time-0preferences, which we refer to asmyopic Pareto optimality, we introduce
the notion ofdynamic Pareto-optimalallocation processes that takes into account the dynamic
structure of risk profiles in the decision making process. We show that such dynamic Pareto-
optimal allocation processes can be constructed recursively backwards in time, starting with the
allocation at the terminal time, and that the allocation at each time point is the solution to a social
welfare optimization problem.
Furthermore, we extend the classical notion of comonotonicity to the dynamic setting, and we
derive a dynamic comonotone improvement theorem for allocation processes. This motivates the
study of dynamic Pareto optima in a comonotone dynamic market. We provide a crisp character-
ization of Pareto optima when agent preferences are coherent and satisfy a property that we call
equidistribution-preserving, and we provide a clear and easily implementable recursive algorithm
for finding these optima. In the special case of the single period problem, we recover the char-

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
This document introduces the concept of "dynamic Pareto optima" in multi-period pure-exchange economies. The main points covered are:

*   **Problem Setting:** The study focuses on economies with discrete time periods where agents have preferences over stochastic endowment processes. These preferences are represented by "strongly time-consistent dynamic risk measures."
*   **Dynamic Pareto Optimality:** The paper defines and introduces the notion of "dynamic Pareto-optimal allocation processes," which differ from traditional static Pareto optimality by incorporating the dynamic structure of risk profiles.
*   **Recursive Construction:** A key result is that dynamic Pareto-optimal allocations can be constructed recursively, starting from the allocation at the terminal time and working backward.
*   **Comonotone Improvement Theorem:** The document derives a "comonotone improvement theorem" for allocation processes.
*   **Characterization of Comonotone Dynamic Pareto Optima:** It provides a recursive approach to constructing comonotone dynamic Pareto optima, particularly when agent preferences are "coherent" and "equidistribution-preserving."
*   **Special Case: Distortion Type Risk Measures:** For agents whose dynamic risk measures are of the "distortion type," a closed-form characterization of comonotone dynamic Pareto optima is provided.
*   **Illustration:** The results are illustrated with a specific example in a two-period setting, highlighting the differences between dynamic and static models and the impact of future risks on earlier allocations.
*   **Contrast with Existing Literature:** The paper argues that existing literature often adopts a myopic view by discounting future outcomes to time zero. The proposed dynamic approach aims to capture the full dynamic structure of endowment profiles.
*   **Assumptions:** Agents' preferences are assumed to be (conditionally) translation invariant, a standard assumption for risk measures, and admit a recursive representation.
*   **Structure:** The paper outlines its structure, including sections on notation, problem definition, characterization of Pareto optima, comonotone Pareto optima, a numerical example, and conclusions.

structure.title: The Dynamic Optimal-Allocation Problem
structure.summary:
This document introduces a novel approach to defining Pareto optimality in multi-period pure-exchange economies, moving beyond traditional time-0 preference-based efficiency. The core of the paper lies in the concept of **dynamic Pareto optimality**, which incorporates the dynamic structure of risk profiles into decision-making.

Key points covered include:

*   **Critique of Myopic Efficiency:** The paper argues that existing literature on optimal consumption and allocations in dynamic frameworks, which discounts future streams to time-0, leads to an inherently myopic view that ignores the dynamic nature of endowments and risks.
*   **Introduction of Dynamic Risk Measures:** The authors propose using dynamic risk measures to incorporate the dynamic structure of risk profiles into decision-making.
*   **Dynamic Individual Rationality and Pareto Optimality:** Based on dynamic risk measures, the paper introduces new notions of dynamic individual rationality and dynamic Pareto optimality.
*   **Formal Definitions:** The document provides formal definitions for myopic Pareto optimality (which considers only time-0 risk) and dynamic Pareto optimality (which considers risk at all future time points).
*   **Characterization of Dynamic Pareto Optima:** A key result (Theorem 4.3) shows that a dynamic allocation is Pareto optimal if and only if it is the solution to a series of backward-in-time optimization problems.
*   **Comonotonicity in Dynamic Settings:** The paper extends the concept of comonotonicity to the dynamic setting and derives a comonotone improvement theorem for dynamic risk measures. It also studies Pareto optima in a comonotone market.

nodes.title: Allocations in a Single-Period Model
nodes.summary:
This partial document, an appendix to a paper on "Dynamic Pareto Optima in Multi-Period Pure-Exchange Economies," focuses on the static, single-period setting of optimal allocation problems. It defines key concepts:

*   **Allocation:** A redistribution of initial endowments among agents such that the sum of individual holdings equals the aggregate endowment.
*   **Individual Rationality:** An allocation is individually rational if no agent is worse off than with their initial endowment, as measured by their static risk measure.
*   **Pareto Optimality:** An allocation is Pareto optimal if no other individually rational allocation can make at least one agent better off without making any other agent worse off.
*   **Comonotone Pareto Optimality:** A refinement of Pareto optimality that considers only comonotone allocations, where agents' payoffs move in the same direction.

The appendix also references seminal results concerning Pareto optima for translation-invariant risk measures and the comonotone improvement theorem.
